\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Background}
The Isolation Lemma is one of the most versatile probabilistic tools in
theoretical computer science. Given a set system --- a family $\mathcal{F}$ of
subsets of a ground set $V$ of size $n$ --- and a random weighting
$w : V \to \{1,\dots,N\}$, the minimum-weight member of $\mathcal{F}$ (where the
weight of a set is the sum of its elements' weights) is unique with probability
at least $1 - n/N$. This isolation of a unique optimum underlies parallel
algorithms for perfect matching, the Valiant--Vazirani reduction from
\textsc{Sat} to \textsc{UniqueSat}, and numerous derandomization and
complexity-theoretic constructions.

Behind the probabilistic statement lies a purely combinatorial counting
question: exactly how many weight assignments isolate a unique minimum-weight
member? Faber and Harris (2018) sharpened the picture by proving a tight lower
bound on this count, uniform across all inclusion-free hypergraphs. This raises
the extremal question: is the lower bound ever attained exactly, and by what
structure? We answer it completely for the canonical case.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item An exact closed-form count of the isolating assignments for the singleton
  hypergraph with zero offset, equal to $n \cdot \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{\,n-1}$
  (Theorem~\ref{thm:main}).
  \item A proof that the ``$\exists!$ minimum'' notion of isolation and the
  ``strict minimum'' formulation coincide (Proposition~\ref{prop:equiv}).
  \item Global tightness of the Faber--Harris lower bound, with the singleton
  hypergraph as explicit extremal witness (Corollary~\ref{cor:tight}).
  \item Numerical verification, boundary analysis, and precise conjectures for the
  general per-hypergraph tightness problem (Section~\ref{sec:future}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Definitions}

Throughout, $n$ (vertices) and $d$ (weight values) are natural numbers. We write
$[n] = \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ and $[d] = \{0,1,\dots,d-1\}$.

\begin{definition}[Weight assignment]
A \emph{weight assignment} is a function $w : [n] \to [d]$. There are exactly
$d^n$ such assignments.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Hypergraph]
A \emph{hypergraph} on $[n]$ is a finite family $H$ of subsets (``edges'') of
$[n]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Inclusion-free / Sperner]
A hypergraph $H$ is \emph{inclusion-free} (a \emph{Sperner family} or
\emph{antichain}) if $S,T \in H$ and $S \subseteq T$ imply $S = T$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Edge offset and edge weight]
An \emph{edge offset} is a function $f : H \to \mathbb{R}$. Under an assignment
$w$, the weight of an edge $S \in H$ is
\[
\wt_{w,f}(S) = f(S) + \sum_{v \in S} w(v).
\]
The \emph{zero offset} is $f \equiv 0$, giving $\wt_{w,0}(S) = \sum_{v \in S} w(v)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Isolating assignment]
An assignment $w$ is \emph{isolating} for $(H,f)$ if a unique edge $S \in H$
attains $\min_{T \in H} \wt_{w,f}(T)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Singleton hypergraph]
The \emph{singleton hypergraph} on $[n]$ is
$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}} = \{\{v\} : v \in [n]\}$.
\end{definition}

For the singleton hypergraph with zero offset, $\wt_{w,0}(\{v\}) = w(v)$, so an
assignment is isolating exactly when a unique vertex attains the minimum vertex
weight. This reduction makes the singleton case the cleanest model of the general
lemma.

\section{Two formulations of isolation}

\begin{definition}
For $w : [n] \to [d]$:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $w$ has a \emph{unique argmin} if $\exists!\, i \in [n]$ with
  $w(i) \le w(j)$ for all $j$;
  \item $w$ has a \emph{strict minimum} if $\exists\, i \in [n]$ with
  $w(i) < w(j)$ for all $j \neq i$.
\end{itemize}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Equivalence]\label{prop:equiv}
For every assignment $w$, $w$ has a unique argmin if and only if $w$ has a strict
minimum.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Let $i$ be the unique argmin. For $j \neq i$, if $w(i) = w(j)$
then $w(j) = w(i) \le w(k)$ for all $k$, making $j$ an argmin and contradicting
uniqueness; hence $w(i) < w(j)$, so $i$ is a strict minimum.

($\Leftarrow$) Let $i$ be a strict minimum. Then $w(i) \le w(j)$ for all $j$, so
$i$ is an argmin. If $k$ is also an argmin with $k \neq i$, then $w(i) < w(k)$
contradicts $w(k) \le w(i)$; hence $k = i$.
\end{proof}

By Proposition~\ref{prop:equiv} we use the strict-minimum formulation. Define
\[
\mathrm{Iso}(n,d) = \{ w : [n] \to [d] \mid w \text{ has a strict minimum}\},
\]
and for a fixed $i \in [n]$,
\[
\mathrm{SM}_i(n,d) = \{ w : [n] \to [d] \mid w(i) < w(j)\ \forall j \neq i \}.
\]

\section{Main results}

\begin{theorem}[Exact count]\label{thm:main}
For all natural numbers $n,d$,
\[
|\mathrm{Iso}(n,d)| = n \cdot \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{\,n-1},
\]
where $n-1$ is truncated natural subtraction.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Global tightness]\label{cor:tight}
The universal lower bound
$\#\{\text{isolating assignments}\} \ge n \cdot \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{\,n-1}$, valid
for every inclusion-free hypergraph on $n$ vertices under every offset, is
attained with equality by $H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}$ under the zero offset. Hence the
bound cannot be improved.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}$ is inclusion-free: distinct singletons are incomparable and
$\{v\} \subseteq \{w\}$ forces $v = w$. Its isolating assignments under zero
offset are exactly $\mathrm{Iso}(n,d)$, whose cardinality is the bound value by
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Tail count]\label{lem:tail}
For a fixed $m \in [d]$, the number of values in $[d]$ strictly greater than $m$
is $d - 1 - m$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The values are $m+1,\dots,d-1$, of which there are $d-1-m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Fiber count]\label{lem:fiber}
Fix $i \in [n]$ and $m \in [d]$. The number of assignments $w$ with $w(i) = m$ and
$w(j) > m$ for all $j \neq i$ equals $(d-1-m)^{\,n-1}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The set of such assignments is the product $\prod_j T_j$ with $T_i = \{m\}$ and
$T_j = \{v \in [d] : v > m\}$ for $j \neq i$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:tail},
$|T_j| = d-1-m$ for each of the $n-1$ indices $j \neq i$, and $|T_i| = 1$. The
cardinality of a product of finite sets is the product of the cardinalities,
giving $(d-1-m)^{\,n-1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Per-vertex count]\label{lem:pervertex}
For every $i \in [n]$,
\[
|\mathrm{SM}_i(n,d)| = \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{\,n-1},
\]
independent of $i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Partition $\mathrm{SM}_i(n,d)$ by the value $m = w(i)$. Each part is the fiber of
Lemma~\ref{lem:fiber}, so
$|\mathrm{SM}_i(n,d)| = \sum_{m=0}^{d-1} (d-1-m)^{\,n-1}$. Re-indexing by
$k = d-1-m$ (a bijection of $\{0,\dots,d-1\}$ onto itself) gives
$\sum_{k=0}^{d-1} k^{\,n-1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Disjoint decomposition]\label{lem:decomp}
$\mathrm{Iso}(n,d) = \bigsqcup_{i \in [n]} \mathrm{SM}_i(n,d)$, hence
$|\mathrm{Iso}(n,d)| = \sum_{i \in [n]} |\mathrm{SM}_i(n,d)|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$w \in \mathrm{Iso}(n,d)$ iff $w$ has a strict minimum at some vertex $i$, i.e.
$w \in \mathrm{SM}_i(n,d)$ for some $i$. The union is disjoint: if
$w \in \mathrm{SM}_i \cap \mathrm{SM}_{i'}$ with $i \neq i'$, then $w(i) < w(i')$
and $w(i') < w(i)$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]
By Lemmas~\ref{lem:decomp} and \ref{lem:pervertex},
\[
|\mathrm{Iso}(n,d)| = \sum_{i \in [n]} |\mathrm{SM}_i(n,d)|
= \sum_{i \in [n]} \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{\,n-1}
= n \cdot \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{\,n-1}. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\section{Algorithms}

\textbf{Algorithm A --- Direct enumeration.} Iterate over all $d^n$ assignments;
for each, compute the minimum value and test whether exactly one vertex attains
it. Time $\Theta(n \cdot d^n)$; used for verification on small parameters.

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{Algorithm B --- Closed-form evaluation.} Return
$n \cdot \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{\,n-1}$ directly. With fast exponentiation this uses
$O(d \log n)$ arithmetic operations, exponentially faster than enumeration.

\section{Numerical verification and boundary analysis}

Direct enumeration matches the closed form for all $(n,d)$ with $0 \le n \le 4$,
$1 \le d \le 5$. Representative values for $n = 3$:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrr}
\toprule
$d$ & $\sum_{j<d} j^2$ & $|\mathrm{Iso}(3,d)|$ & total $d^3$ \\
\midrule
1 & 0  & 0  & 1   \\
2 & 1  & 3  & 8   \\
3 & 5  & 15 & 27  \\
4 & 14 & 42 & 64  \\
5 & 30 & 90 & 125 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\paragraph{Boundary cases.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item $n = 0$: no vertex, so $|\mathrm{Iso}(0,d)| = 0$; the factor $n=0$ makes
  the closed form vanish.
  \item $n = 1$: the lone vertex is vacuously a strict minimum, so all $d$
  assignments are isolating; the closed form gives
  $1 \cdot \sum_{j<d} j^0 = d$.
  \item $d = 1$, $n \ge 2$: all vertices share the single value, no strict minimum
  exists, count $0$; the closed form gives $n \cdot 0^{\,n-1} = 0$, certifying the
  count is genuine.
\end{itemize}

\section{Discussion and future directions}\label{sec:future}

The exact count shows the Faber--Harris lower bound is attained on the nose by a
concrete inclusion-free hypergraph, and reveals its combinatorial meaning: the
factor $n$ enumerates the unique argmin vertex, the summand $j^{\,n-1}$ is the
fiber size over a fixed argmin, and the sum ranges over the minimum value.

\begin{conjecture}[Per-hypergraph tightness]
For every inclusion-free hypergraph $H$ on $n$ vertices there is an offset $f$ so
that the number of isolating assignments in $[d]^n$ equals exactly
$n \cdot \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{\,n-1}$. A generic offset should flatten $H$'s
internal comparisons so that isolation is governed by a single controlling vertex
per assignment.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Rigidity of extremizers]
The offsets $f$ achieving the exact minimum count form a positive-measure,
polyhedrally described region, and every extremizer induces the same
argmin-partition statistics as the singleton hypergraph.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Strict gap away from Sperner families]
If $H$ is not inclusion-free, then for every offset $f$ the number of isolating
assignments is strictly less than $n \cdot \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{\,n-1}$ for all
sufficiently large $d$, because a containment $S \subsetneq T$ couples two edges'
weights and destroys the independence the extremal count relies on.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Refined power-sum decomposition]
For every $n$, the extremal count $n \cdot \sum_{j<d} j^{n-1}$, as a polynomial in
$d$, has its nonnegative-integer roots at $d = 0,1$, and its leading behavior
reflects a bijective decomposition of isolating assignments by (argmin vertex,
minimum value).
\end{conjecture}

\section{Conclusion}

We established the exact number of isolating weight assignments for the singleton
hypergraph under zero offset, $n \cdot \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{\,n-1}$, proving that
the sharp Faber--Harris lower bound is globally tight and exhibiting an explicit
extremal witness. The proof is a transparent fiberwise decomposition that
explains each factor of the extremal formula, and it motivates a concrete program
for understanding tightness across all inclusion-free hypergraphs under arbitrary
edge offsets.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Ground truth: direct enumeration (Algorithm A)

def enumerate_isolating(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Count isolating assignments in [d]^n by exhaustive enumeration.

    Time complexity Theta(n * d^n); intended for small parameters only.
    """
    if n == 0:

    count = 0
    for w in product(range(d), repeat=n):

def closed_form(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Return n * sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^(n-1) using truncated (natural) subtraction.

    For n == 0 the leading factor nullifies the sum, so the value is 0.
    Note 0**0 == 1 in Python, matching the natural-number convention.
    """
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    exponent = n - 1
    return n * sum(j ** exponent for j in range(d))

def per_vertex_count(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Number of assignments for which a FIXED vertex i is the strict minimum.

    Equals sum_{m=0}^{d-1} (d-1-m)^(n-1) = sum_{k=0}^{d-1} k^(n-1),
    independent of i.
    """
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    exponent = n - 1
    return sum((d - 1 - m) ** exponent for m in range(d))


def fiber_count(n: int, d: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Number of assignments with a fixed argmin vertex taking minimum value m:
    the argmin is fixed, and each of the other n-1 vertices exceeds m.
    Equals (d - 1 - m)^(n-1)."""
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    return (d - 1 - m) ** (n - 1)

    return sum(fiber_count(n, d, m) for _ in range(n) for m in range(d))

    "demo": """"
Numerical demonstration of the Exact Count Theorem for the Isolation Lemma.

For n vertices, each weighted from {0, 1, ..., d-1}, an assignment
w = (w_0, ..., w_{n-1}) is called *isolating* when a single vertex attains the
strict minimum weight (i.e. there is a unique index i with w_i < w_j for all
j != i).

Main result (Exact Count Theorem):

    #{ isolating assignments } = n * sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^(n-1),

which is exactly the Faber-Harris universal lower bound for inclusion-free
hypergraphs -- so the singleton hypergraph attains that bound term for term.

This script cross-checks the closed form against brute-force enumeration and
against the fiberwise decomposition (argmin vertex x minimum value), and
illustrates the boundary cases.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Iterator, List, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Ground truth: direct enumeration (Algorithm A)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def enumerate_isolating(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Count isolating assignments in [d]^n by exhaustive enumeration.

    Time complexity Theta(n * d^n); intended for small parameters only.
    """
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    count = 0
    for w in product(range(d), repeat=n):
        m = min(w)
        if sum(1 for x in w if x == m) == 1:
            count += 1
    return count


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Closed form: the Exact Count Theorem (Algorithm B)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def closed_form(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Return n * sum_{j=0}^{d-1} j^(n-1) using truncated (natural) subtraction.

    For n == 0 the leading factor nullifies the sum, so the value is 0.
    Note 0**0 == 1 in Python, matching the natural-number convention.
    """
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    exponent = n - 1
    return n * sum(j ** exponent for j in range(d))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Fiberwise decomposition (the proof, made computational)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def per_vertex_count(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Number of assignments for which a FIXED vertex i is the strict minimum.

    Equals sum_{m=0}^{d-1} (d-1-m)^(n-1) = sum_{k=0}^{d-1} k^(n-1),
    independent of i.
    """
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    exponent = n - 1
    return sum((d - 1 - m) ** exponent for m in range(d))


def fiber_count(n: int, d: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Number of assignments with a fixed argmin vertex taking minimum value m:
    the argmin is fixed, and each of the other n-1 vertices exceeds m.
    Equals (d - 1 - m)^(n-1)."""
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    return (d - 1 - m) ** (n - 1)


def decomposition_total(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Reconstruct the total via the (argmin vertex, minimum value) fibering."""
    return sum(fiber_count(n, d, m) for _ in range(n) for m in range(d))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reporting helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def grid(n_range: range, d_range: range) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, int]]:
    for n in n_range:
        for d in d_range:
            yield n, d


def verify_grid(n_range: range, d_range: range) -> bool:
    ok = True
    for n, d in grid(n_range, d_range):
        e = enumerate_isolating(n, d)
        c = closed_form(n, d)
        f = decomposition_total(n, d)
        agree = (e == c == f)
        ok = ok and agree
        flag = "OK " if agree else "!! "
        print(f"  {flag}n={n} d={d}: enum={e:>6}  closed={c:>6}  fiber={f:>6}")
    return ok


def sequence_row(n: int, d_max: int) -> List[int]:
    return [closed_form(n, d) for d in range(d_max + 1)]


def main() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Exact Count Theorem for the Isolation Lemma (singleton hypergraph)")
    print("   #isolating(n,d) = n * sum_{j<d} j^(n-1)")
    print("=" * 68)

    print("\n[1] Cross-check over a grid (enumeration vs closed form vs fibering):")
    all_ok = verify_grid(range(0, 5), range(1, 6))
    print(f"\n   ==> all agree: {all_ok}")

    print("\n[2] Worked example n=3, d=4:")
    print("   3 * (0^2 + 1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2) = 3 * 14 = 42")
    print(f"   closed_form(3,4)         = {closed_form(3, 4)}")
    print(f"   enumerate_isolating(3,4) = {enumerate_isolating(3, 4)}")
    print(f"   total assignments 4^3    = {4 ** 3}")

    print("\n[3] Per-vertex fiber size (independent of the chosen vertex):")
    for i in range(3):
        print(f"   vertex i={i}: strict-min-at-i count = {per_vertex_count(3, 4)}")
    print("   (each equals sum_{j<4} j^2 = 14, and 3 * 14 = 42)")

    print("\n[4] Isolating-count sequences n * sum_{j<d} j^(n-1):")
    for n in range(1, 5):
        print(f"   n={n}: {sequence_row(n, 6)}")

    print("\n[5] Boundary cases:")
    print(f"   n=0 (no vertices):       closed={closed_form(0,5)} enum={enumerate_isolating(0,5)}")
    print(f"   n=1 (single vertex, d=5): closed={closed_form(1,5)} enum={enumerate_isolating(1,5)} (=d)")
    print(f"   d=1, n=3 (one value):    closed={closed_form(3,1)} enum={enumerate_isolating(3,1)}")

    print("\nDone.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import Mathlib
import Catalog.Novelty.NeuralCoding

/-!
# Neural Coding III: the Weight Distribution and Energy Concentration

This file deepens the neural-coding theory of `Catalog/Novelty/NeuralCoding.lean`.
That file computed the *first moment* of the metabolic weight (energy) of a
dense code — the average number of active neurons is `N / 2`.  Here we compute
the **full concentration profile** of the weight, bridging the exact
combinatorics of binary patterns with a probabilistic (measure-concentration)
conclusion.

## Model

We reuse the type `NeuralCode N = Fin N → Bool` and the `weight` (= metabolic
energy) of a code, the number of active neurons.  Regarding all `2 ^ N` codes as
equally likely, `weight` is a random variable and we study its spread.

## Results (the chain)

1. `card_active_pair` — a *fixed pair* of distinct neurons `i ≠ j` is jointly
   active in exactly `2 ^ (N - 2)` codes (a second-order refinement of the
   first-order symmetry `NeuralCoding.card_active_coord`).
2. `sum_weight_sq` — the exact **second moment**: summed over all codes,
   `∑ (weight c)² = 2 ^ N · N (N+1) / 4` (uses 1 and `card_active_coord`).
3. `sum_weight_centered_sq` — the exact **total squared deviation** from the
   mean `N / 2`: `∑ (weight c − N/2)² = N · 2 ^ N / 4` (uses 2 and the first
   moment `NeuralCoding.total_weight`).
4. `weight_variance` — the **variance** of a dense code's weight is exactly
   `N / 4` (the binomial variance `N p (1-p)` at `p = 1/2`) (uses 3).
5. `weight_concentration` — a **Chebyshev concentration bound**: the fraction of
   codes whose weight deviates from `N / 2` by at least `t` is at most
   `N / (4 t²)` (uses 3).
6. `most_codes_near_half` — a concrete corollary: at least three quarters of all
   codes have weight within `√N` of `N / 2`.  Dense neural activity concentrates
   sharply around the half-active state (uses 5).

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): the average energy `N / 2` established earlier hides
the more interesting fact that *almost all* codes are close to it — the
population energy is sharply concentrated.  We conjectured the weight behaves
like a Binomial(N, 1/2), so its variance should be exactly `N / 4` and Chebyshev
should give `O(1/t²)` tails, with a `√N`-window capturing a constant fraction.

Experiment (Experimenter): the crux is the exact second moment.  Writing
`weight = ∑_i 1[c i]`, we have `weight² = ∑_i ∑_j 1[c i] 1[c j]`; summing over
codes turns each term into a *joint* activity count.  The diagonal contributes
`2^(N-1)` (single-neuron symmetry, imported from the capacity file) and each of
the `N (N-1)` off-diagonal terms contributes `2^(N-2)` (`card_active_pair`).
Small cases `N = 0, 1` were checked to confirm the closed form has no boundary
defect.  Chebyshev then follows by discarding the codes inside the window and
bounding each retained squared deviation below by `t²`.

Analysis (Analyst): the identity `4 ∑ (weight)² = 2^N N (N+1)` is boundary-clean
(true for every `N`, including the degenerate `N = 0, 1`) precisely because the
`N (N-1)` prefactor annihilates the pair term exactly when no pair exists.  The
variance `N / 4` is the algebraic fingerprint of independence of the `N`
coordinates; the concentration bound is the probabilistic shadow of that
algebra.

Critique (Critic): the concentration statement is non-vacuous — the `√N`-window
corollary exhibits an explicit constant fraction (`3/4`), so the tail bound is
not hollow.  The hypothesis `0 < t` in Chebyshev is load-bearing (division by
`t²`), and `1 ≤ N` in the corollary guarantees the window `√N` is positive.

Synthesis (PI): the weight of a dense code is a Binomial(N, 1/2) in disguise;
its first two moments (`N/2`, variance `N/4`) and the resulting `1/√N`-scale
concentration mean that dense coding not only *spends* `N/2` spikes on average
but does so with vanishing relative fluctuation — a metabolic law of large
numbers for neural populations.
-/

namespace NeuralWeightConcentration

open Finset NeuralCoding

/-! ## 0. Weight as a sum of indicators -/

/--
The weight of a code is the sum over neurons of the `0/1` activity indicator.
-/
theorem weight_eq_sum_indicator {N : ℕ} (c : NeuralCode N) :
    weight c = ∑ i : Fin N, (if c i = true then 1 else 0) := by
  convert Finset.card_filter ( fun i => c i = true ) Finset.univ using 1

/-! ## 1. Joint activity of a pair of neurons -/

/--
**Second-order symmetry.**  Two distinct neurons `i ≠ j` are simultaneously
active in exactly `2 ^ (N - 2)` of the `2 ^ N` codes: fixing two coordinates to
`true` leaves the other `N - 2` free.
-/
theorem card_active_pair {N : ℕ} (i j : Fin N) (hij : i ≠ j) :
    (Finset.univ.filter (fun c : NeuralCode N => c i = true ∧ c j = true)).card
      = 2 ^ (N - 2) := by
  have h_card : Finset.card (Finset.univ.filter fun c : Fin N → Bool => c i = true ∧ c j = true) = Finset.card (Finset.univ.filter fun c : Fin N → Bool => c i = true) / 2 := by

# Computational Evidence — Weight Distribution of Binary Neural Codes

We model a neural code on `N` neurons as a binary activity pattern and let the
**weight** be the number of active neurons. Regarding all `2^N` patterns as
equally likely, the weight is a random variable. This note records the
small-case data that motivated and confirmed the closed forms proved in
`NeuralWeightConcentration.lean`.

## 1. Exact moment sums (brute force over all `2^N` patterns)

For each `N` we enumerated all `2^N` patterns and summed the weight and the
squared weight.

| N | ∑ weight | N·2^(N-1) | 4·∑ weight² | 2^N·N(N+1) |
|---|----------|-----------|-------------|------------|
| 0 | 0        | 0         | 0           | 0          |
| 1 | 1        | 1         | 4           | 4          |
| 2 | 4        | 4         | 24          | 24         |
| 3 | 12       | 12        | 96          | 96         |
| 4 | 32       | 32        | 320         | 320        |
| 5 | 80       | 80        | 960         | 960        |

Both closed forms match exactly for every `N` tested:

* First moment: `∑ weight = N·2^(N-1)`, i.e. mean `= N/2`.
* Second moment: `4·∑ weight² = 2^N·N(N+1)`, i.e. `E[weight²] = N(N+1)/4`.

## 2. Centred second moment and variance

| N | ∑ (weight − N/2)² | N·2^N/4 | variance = (∑ …)/2^N | N/4 |
|---|-------------------|---------|----------------------|-----|
| 0 | 0                 | 0       | 0                    | 0   |
| 1 | 0.5               | 0.5     | 0.25                 | 0.25|
| 2 | 2                 | 2       | 0.5                  | 0.5 |
| 3 | 6                 | 6       | 0.75                 | 0.75|
| 4 | 16                | 16      | 1                    | 1   |
| 5 | 40                | 40      | 1.25                 | 1.25|

The variance is exactly `N/4` in every case — the Binomial `N·p·(1−p)`
variance at `p = 1/2`.

## 3. Sequence identification

The average-weight numerators `0, 1, 4, 12, 32, 80, …` are `N·2^(N-1)`
(OEIS A001787). The second-moment numerators `0, 1, 6, 24, 80, 240, …`
follow `2^(N-2)·N·(N+1)`. Both are elementary and index cleanly, so no deeper
sequence search was needed.

## 4. Counterexample hunt

We searched for any `N ≤ 12` violating `4·∑ weight² = 2^N·N(N+1)` or
`variance = N/4`; none was found. The `√N`-window fraction
`#{|weight − N/2| < √N} / 2^N` was checked to stay above `3/4` for
`1 ≤ N ≤ 12`, consistent with the Chebyshev corollary.

All closed forms are therefore supported by exhaustive small-case data before
being established in general.

# Future Directions — Neural Coding: from Averages to Concentration

The present cycle upgraded the neural-coding chain from *first-moment* facts
(capacity `2^N`, average energy `N/2`, sparse counts `C(N,k)`, population
precision `1/√N`) to a *full concentration* statement: the metabolic weight of a
dense code has variance exactly `N/4`, and at least three quarters of all codes
lie within `√N` of the mean `N/2`. The weight is a Binomial(N, 1/2) in disguise,
so the population energy obeys a law of large numbers. The following conjectures
push this "moments → concentration → geometry" programme further.

## 1. Sub-Gaussian (exponential) energy concentration

**Conjecture.** The fraction of codes whose weight deviates from `N/2` by at
least `t` decays like `exp(−2t²/N)`, not merely `N/(4t²)`; consequently, for any
fixed `ε > 0`, all but an exponentially small fraction of codes have weight in
`[(1/2−ε)N, (1/2+ε)N]`.

The key insight is that the coordinates of a binary code are independent bounded
contributions, so the weight is not just a variance-`N/4` variable but a genuine
sum of independent `±` increments, and the exponential moment — not the second
moment — is the sharp instrument. Chebyshev sees only the second moment; the
correct object is the log-moment-generating function of a single neuron.

Why now? The exact second moment established this cycle is the first term of the
cumulant expansion; having pinned it down, the natural next step is to control
the whole cumulant sequence and convert the polynomial tail into an exponential
one, which immediately sharpens every downstream capacity estimate.

## 2. Energy–distance trade-off for noise-tolerant codebooks

**Conjecture.** Any codebook with minimum Hamming distance `d` whose codewords
all have weight near `N/2` (within `o(√N)`) satisfies a strictly stronger size
bound than the generic Singleton ceiling `2^(N+1−d)`; concentrating the energy
budget forces the codewords into a thin equatorial shell whose limited volume
caps the codebook.

The key insight is that the concentration result says the overwhelming majority
of patterns already live near the equator, so a large-distance codebook cannot
also be energy-balanced without competing for the *same* scarce shell that
carries most of the mass — packing and balancing pull against each other.

Why now? With both the Singleton projection ceiling and the exact weight
concentration in hand, the two constraints can finally be imposed
simultaneously, turning a qualitative tension into a quantitative shell-volume
bound.

## 3. Concentration of the population-coding error

**Conjecture.** When `N` neurons independently estimate a stimulus, not only
does the mean squared error scale like `1/N`, but the *realised* error
concentrates around its mean: the probability that the population estimate is off
by more than `c/√N` decays polynomially in `N` for every constant `c`, so the
`1/√N` precision law holds pattern-by-pattern, not only on average.

The key insight is that the same variance-of-the-mean algebra that produced the
`1/√N` law also controls the fourth moment of the averaged estimate, and a
second-moment bound on the *squared* error upgrades an average guarantee into a
high-probability one.

Why now? The population-precision law and the weight-variance computation share
one algebraic engine — the independence of the `N` contributions — so the
concentration machinery just proved for weights transfers directly to the
estimator error.

## 4. Dimension of the concentrated neural manifold

**Conjecture.** If population activity is driven by `d` behavioural degrees of
freedom through a generic bounded map, then not only is the neural manifold's
dimension at most `d`, but the reachable activity concentrates on an
`d`-dimensional shell of radius `Θ(√N)`; the effective, energy-weighted
dimension is exactly `d` even though the ambient space has dimension `N`.

The key insight is that concentration of the raw activity (weights near `N/2`)
and the linear-algebraic dimension cap combine: the manifold is not merely
low-dimensional but sits at a fixed metabolic radius, so its "thickness" in the
energy direction vanishes relative to `√N`.

Why now? The dimension bound and the energy concentration were proved
separately; overlaying them is the natural synthesis, and it predicts a testable
geometric signature — a fixed-radius, low-dimensional activity shell — for
recorded population data.
